The green flash that imprints on the back of your eyes, right as the sun dips into the horizon—that’s Ragtime.
The considerable beauty of this inspiriting show — full of complicated emotions about our diaspora nation — is streaked with melancholy.

Whether "Ragtime" is presented in productions mammoth (as in its 1998 premiere) or modest (the 2009 revival), the musical, adapted from E.L. Doctorow's kaleidoscopic 1975 novel, reverberates with the directness, passion and allegorical heft of an American folk epic.
What he delivers in Ragtime is, quite simply, some of the most magnificent singing I have ever heard on Broadway

DeBessonet takes the challenge and wins, rescuing a near-classic from the excesses of the 1990s to prove, once and for all, that Ragtime, imperfect as it may be, deserves a place among the most significant musical theater achievements of that decade.
Fortunately, the show sounds gloriously lush throughout...So much so that it hardly needs much embellishment at all.
In the end, it was the anthemic score of “Ragtime” (ah, the 1990s) that endeared it to so many theatergoers and that is where the solid new Lincoln Center revival wisely places its focus.
Stripping away the excesses of Lynn Ahrens, Stephen Flaherty and Terrence McNally’s 1996 musical amplifies its many, many flaws.
Revived once again by Lear DeBessonet following last year’s outstanding City Center concert version, this nearly flawless Theater production ranks among Broadway’s best of all time.
Henry is, in a word, magnificent.
This is a magnificent, emotionally charged production that not only honors its source material but thrillingly reaffirms the musical’s place as a defining and urgent American epic.
This production of Ragtime is one of them.

"Rather than a slave of duty, Pirates! is the servant of too many masters: Gilbert & Sullivan, Dixieland jazz, milquetoast liberalism, and the tourism lobby New Orleans & Company, which "kindly sponsored" this production. The recipe is for a jambalaya of disparate flavors that come together in delicious harmony.
Yes, it's sad that 2025 proves to be the right time for "Ragtime," but that doesn't mean you should pass up the chance to witness this truly unforgettable production.
More than a revival, this “Ragtime” feels like a reckoning—urgent, elegant, and profoundly alive.
The melodically thunderous presence of Henry and this phenomenal company—they meld so beautifully as a collective—are the spellbinding reasons to book a ticket pronto.
It’s an ecstatic, gutwrenching, and timely masterpiece by three writers at a pinnacle of their careers.
Ragtime gives us hope to hold onto today, where hope for most of us is a spare commodity.
Between its robust score, showcase moments for the cast, and evergreen resonance, Ragtime is easy to heartily recommend.
"More than thatit is Pirates staged with wonderfully energetic aplomb by director Scott Ellis, wittily choreographed by Warren Carlyle and expertly performed by a dream ensemble.
All that sweetness sours on the tongue and in that, Ragtime justifies its return with unfortunately impeccable timing.

If anything, this musical adaptation of E.L. Doctorow’s novel about the cultural and political upheavals in the New York of the early 1900s, feels even more timely in the midst of the cultural and political upheavals in the America of 2025.
The story is not so much dramatized as it is told to us in a series of Wikipedia lectures.
The great American musical returns: Ragtime‘s latest revival proves its message of social justice remains heartbreakingly relevant today.
And on Broadway, with this glorious company, that song has never sounded more urgent, more human, or more full of hope.
There are very few things that equal the grandeur and pageantry of a perfectly executed, epic Broadway musical.

It is very rare that a revival of a musical is imagined better than the original production and exceptional that its message is more relevant now than when it first opened on Broadway nearly thirty years ago in 1997, garnering four Tony Awards.
For me, Ragtime was a cathartic collective experience, given what we are living through today in our traumatized country.
DeBessonet's thoughtful staging underscores why Ragtime is still worth revisiting.
Musical theatre doesn’t get much better than the dramatic scene and song delivered by “New Music” midway through Act One.

Theater’s revival of Ragtime is Broadway at its very finest, a top-notch production of an American classic with stellar performances, direction, and human themes that touch, entertain, and remain relevant, in their clear connection between then and now.
In fact, there are few musicals more stirring and satisfying when staged and sung as beautifully as “Ragtime” is here.

sg.ra: Thrust stage projects into the audience here, so front-center puts you directly in the actors' playing space with 180-degree eye contact. However, SeatPlan and JK's TheatreScene both warn the thrust's elevated downstage lip can obscure upstage action, and the shallow rake this close means you look up at performers working the far edge of the thrust.

At the middle of the thrust's semicircle, the stadium-style rake lifts you over heads in front while the curved row geometry keeps you square to the playing area — the thrust no longer feels side-on because you're on its central axis. SeatPlan, Headout, TickPick and Broadway Scene all converge on D-K center as the best sightlines in the house.

Sits on the central axis of the thrust so you see the three-sided staging in balance rather than from an angle. LCT's official chart confirms Row P has a dedicated step-up giving it elevation above Row O, and Headout lists L, P, O, K as the value-balance rows. At a thrust stage, back-center beats side-front because you read the full geometry of audience-wrapping blocking.

On a thrust stage, the far-side Orchestra seats end up looking ACROSS the playing space rather than at it — you see actors' profiles and often stare at the back of the thrust's far edge. SeatPlan: 'restricted views depending on staging.' JK's TheatreScene explicitly warns 'avoid the 4 or 5 seats closest to the wall.' BWW Forum thread 1082386 exists specifically because patrons worry about side-seat restriction at this venue.

The elevated Loge wraps the same semicircle as the Orchestra but 2 flights up (LCT: 30 steps), giving you the map-view of the thrust's three-sided blocking that's impossible from Orchestra. TickPick: 'Center, in the first three rows' is premium. SeatPlan confirms 'no bar or obstructions' at the front edge. For a thrust stage this is arguably a better seat than Orchestra for geometry-heavy stagings.

Only 5 rows exist in the Loge, so 'back Loge' is still close. TickPick: 'Rows D and E of Center Left and Center Right offer amazing views at a lower cost.' JK's TheatreScene paid $99 for similar seats and called them 'budget-friendly and worth every penny... view not appreciably different than the first few rows.' Elevated angle reads the thrust's three-sided blocking well even from slight side.

Compounds both weaknesses of a thrust-stage venue: you're on the far side of the semicircle AND at the back of the elevated tier, so the upstage portion of the thrust turns away from you. TickPick names Loge R Row E Seat 509 as the worked example: 'the rear end of the stage is going to be obstructed.' SeatPlan: 'Views from the Loge can feel distant, especially at the far sides.'
